paragraphs.text: A lamp of piety, a proclamation of the knowledge of God: such is the light of the divinely inspired teaching of the Scriptures. For the teaching of the Scriptures is the spring of piety and the beginning of truth, the confidence of the saints and the hope of the faithful, the freedom of the inhabited world and the salvation of the universe. The heavenly lights do not shine on the sky as brightly as the words of God shine on our souls. The variety of fruits does not crown the earth as richly as the teaching of the Scriptures crowns our souls. Springs and rivers do not pour out their streams as abundantly as the teachings of the Holy Spirit gush forth in clear and pure currents. That is why Scripture likens the divine oracles to pure, clear springs, saying: "Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation." And notice the insight of this all-wise teaching and how apt it is: it speaks of a spring, and it commands us to draw. It calls the teachings springs because grace is spread out freely; it commands us to draw because the work is laborious. And since springs we can see have their water at the surface, while the Scriptures hold their meanings in the depths, it did not say "take" or "scoop up," but "draw." What is drawn is drawn from the depths: "Deep water is in a man's heart, but a wise man will draw it out." "Let us draw water with joy." What does "Let us draw with joy" mean? It means: let us labor and rejoice, since all labor is wearisome to the one who labors, but the study of the divine oracles, even if it involves labor, makes the toil sweet. It says: "Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation." The words of the Gospel are the springs of salvation. Before them were the ancient springs, and the words of the prophets were called the springs of Israel. For the words of the prophets belonged to the ancient people alone, while the new springs of the apostles were poured out over the whole world. The first springs are the springs of Israel; the new springs are the springs of salvation. Concerning the ancient springs David says: "In the assemblies bless God the Lord from the springs of Israel"; concerning the new, Isaiah says: "Draw water from the springs of salvation." And what is this salvation? Simeon explains it in the Gospel. When he received the infant who is salvation into his arms, and held in his hands the one who holds all things, he looked not at the visible form of the body but at the hidden dignity of the Godhead, and holding the one who bears all things he said: "Now, Master, you let your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation."

Let us come, then, to one of the springs of salvation, the blessed John the Baptist, so that the word of our humble self may also do justice to the passages just read. John said to those who were coming to be baptized by him: "Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" A strange announcement for a teacher, a strange turn for saving teaching: he insults and does good at once, he threatens and brings good news. "Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee?" If we are fleeing the wrath at all, how are we a brood of vipers? Yet he both calls them a brood and proclaims salvation to them, so that by the name "viper" he might show their former state, and by "fleeing the wrath" he might explain the fruit of repentance. "Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee?" It is as if he said: "Who showed you the way of salvation, when you are unworthy to be saved?" Why do you both teach and insult, show the way and rebuke? It was you who taught us to flee, you who say, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near." But think of someone who wants to make a person who has escaped punishment aware of the wrath he has escaped: he sets before him what he deserved, so that he may learn what he has been granted. "Do you not know," he says, "what danger or punishment you have escaped?" He says it not to reproach him, but to make him aware of the kindness shown to him. "Brood of vipers"—the Baptist says this, and his hearers are not offended. For they were disciples of David, who said: "The righteous man will chasten me in mercy and reprove me." "Bear, then," he says, "fruit worthy of repentance." Explain the "who warned you." Repentance did. If you have run to repentance, bear fruits worthy of repentance. And since he saw them putting on airs at being children of Abraham, he wished to make them understand that it is not a shared lineage that confirms noble birth, but agreement in conduct. So he says: "Bear fruits worthy of repentance, and do not begin to say, 'We have Abraham as our father,'" because lineage does not save one whom his conduct does not save, nor does a shared lineage exalt one whom agreement in conduct does not crown. And so that you may learn that it is of no benefit to have Abraham's lineage without preserving the nobility of his conduct, this saint calls those born of the patriarchs a brood of vipers. He is not insulting the patriarchs or calling them a viper's offspring, but exposing the wickedness of their descendants, just as Isaiah also said to the people descended from Abraham: "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom." He knew them not as kinsmen of the Sodomites but as men of the same conduct, and he spoke so to show that lineage is a matter of conduct: "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give heed to the law of our God, you people of Gomorrah." And the one who said "rulers of Sodom" also says, "Wash yourselves, become clean"—a brother of John indeed, both rebuking and teaching: "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom." Keep this noted on the tablets of your mind, so that when you hear a Jew reproaching you, or saying, "Where do you get the writings of the prophets?" or "Where do you get the right to have Abraham as your father?" you may tell him: "Because the Church takes pride in having Abraham as her father according to faith." If your opponent says, "How are you a son of Abraham?" say to him, "How are you a son of Sodom?" If he says, "Because of the unbelief of the people of that time," you will reply: "If unbelief was able to disgrace noble birth, does faith not transform low birth into nobility?" All the prophets agree with this, honoring conduct and putting lineage second, as Ezekiel said: "Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite; your sister is Sodom." And see the marvel. The Jews might think they were being insulted when they heard themselves called Sodomites, and Judea might seem to be insulted when she heard herself called the sister of Sodom. So the prophet removes her mistaken suspicion and wants to persuade her that she is honored rather than insulted in being called Sodom's sister, since she is called her sister while doing greater evils than she. And since the people took it hard to hear "sister of Sodom," God resolves the doubt, saying: "As I live, says the Lord, your sister Sodom did not commit half of your sins." And see the marvel. Just as a thief is a disgraceful thing in himself, but set beside a robber or a murderer he seems respectable by comparison, so it is with you compared to Sodom. Or rather, by comparison Sodom is more righteous. How so? Scripture says: "Your sister did not sin as you have. As I live, says the Lord, she has been justified by you"—that is, when her deeds are set beside yours, she appears the more respectable.

If, then, the Israelites became worse than the Sodomites, why did they not suffer what the Sodomites suffered? Because God knew the fruits that would spring up from them: apostles, evangelists, preachers, and the very body of salvation that the Benefactor took. He spared the root of ingratitude so as not to cut down the fruits of truth, for, being just, he considered it unjust to cut short the harvest of good things because of a root of wicked men. That is why Isaiah, having said, "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give heed to the law of your God, you people of Gomorrah," goes on to explain why, though they do what the Sodomites did, they do not suffer what the Sodomites suffered. He says: "Your land is desolate, your cities are burned with fire." And: "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." Had the fruit of the apostles not been expected, had God not been awaiting the fruit of the evangelists, had there not been that holy seed which was to come forth from the holy Virgin, we would have become like Sodom. And to show that this is how the saints understood it, and that we are not forcing the meaning, listen to Paul: "Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel; nor are they all children of God because they are the seed of Abraham; but now there is a remnant chosen by grace." What did Isaiah say? "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed." What does the apostle say? "There is a remnant chosen by grace"—not by works. Then he adds: "As Isaiah said, 'Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom.'"

But let us return to our subject. Why does he call the servants of evil snakes? Because of the ancient serpent in paradise. For just as the serpent in paradise became the instrument of the devil's deceit, so now there are many servants of the devil. The devil no longer needs to speak through a snake, since he has many servants. Back then, when he was waging war on Adam and Eve, and there was no other person through whom he could deceive them, since they were alone, he borrowed the form of another kind of creature, and in this way, through them, he deceived many. Now he has no need of a snake, for he has many snakes. Every servant of the devil, every craftsman of wickedness, even if he bears the face of a rational human being, is no different from a snake. For such a man is the devil's instrument, just as the serpent was. That is why the Savior, wishing to show that the one who spoke through the serpent back then was also speaking in the Jews, who at that time were plotting war against God, says to them: "You are of your father the devil, and you want to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and he has not stood in the truth, because he is a liar"; "you are of your father the devil, and you speak what you have heard from him."

Since, then, they were perverting the saving proclamation of the Gospel, the blessed John insults them and exposes the conduct of men who enjoyed benefits and insulted grace by their ingratitude. He says to them: "You snakes, brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear, then, fruits worthy of repentance." Paul does something similar, rebuking while he exhorts: "Reprove," he says, "rebuke, exhort." "And do not begin to say within yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones." Saint John persists in honoring Abraham. He shows God as able to raise up children for him in order to remove the suspicion of the Hebrews: since he had said earlier, "You snakes, brood of vipers," he wanted it understood that he was insulting not the patriarchs but their descendants' conduct. So he says: "Bear fruits worthy of repentance, and do not begin to say, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones." Now for God it is not impossible even to turn a stone into a human being. But Gentiles too were standing by at the holy baptism, watching the miracle and the baptism, as the evangelist says: "All Judea and Samaria went out." So both the Jewish people and the Gentiles were gathered there. That is why he says: "God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones." That is: from these people who are still without feeling, the Gentiles, who have never been worked [?], the hard, the difficult to work with, he is able to raise up children. Pay close attention. Why does he call them stones? Because they worshiped stones, and so made the worshiper like the thing worshiped. That is why David says: "All who worship them become like them, and so do all who trust in them." So John insults those who are slaves to senselessness by likening them to senseless stones.

"Even now the axe is laid at the root of the trees." What a saying, full of fear and love and encouragement! "Even now," he says, "the axe is laid at the root of the trees"—not at work, but threatening. A loving father or teacher, trying to draw a child out of the laziness of childhood, does not strike him, because he wants to spare him; instead he sets the rod down nearby and threatens: "If you don't pay attention to your lessons, you'll have this rod to reckon with," and he holds it, idle yet threatening. In the same way John presents the punishment to come like an axe that is sharpened but does not touch. "Even now the axe is laid at the root of the trees; every tree, therefore, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire." He did not say "that did not bear," since then repentance would have been cut off, but "that does not bear good fruit." He rightly added "good," for one can see other fruits that look fine but are not genuine. "Every tree, therefore, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire." Just as the blessed John brought in the axe, ready but not touching, so David too says to sinners: "If you do not turn back, he will polish his sword." He did not say, "He has polished his sword, he is taking vengeance on his servants, he will strike, he will kill." The sword is being polished now, when you see a prophet saying, "The Lord comes to judgment," and by his word setting forth the coming punishment like a sword on the whetstone, in order to prepare [?] for you; and he displays the fear for this reason, to open for us the way of salvation. "If you do not turn back, he will polish his sword; he has bent his bow and made it ready." He has made the bow ready, yet he does not shoot; instead he shows the stance of an enemy and the affection of a father.

Much more could have been said in reflection on what we have discussed. But the coming of the Holy Spirit, which took place on the holy day of holy Pentecost, draws us on, and we must not pass over the account of it without examining it. The Ascension showed its splendour in its own days and did not stop us from speaking of it afterwards. In the same way, the coming of the Holy Spirit does not stop those who have kept the feast from celebrating even after the feast, from joining the dance of the divine word, and from always enjoying the teaching of the Holy Spirit. "When the day of Pentecost was being fulfilled," it says, "they were all together with one accord in one place." Who were "all"? The apostles and the disciples who were with them. And why did the Holy Spirit come on the day of Pentecost? For this reason. It is not that God is a slave to causes, but that nothing God does is without reason. God appears when he wills, and he wills when he brings about the fitting moment. Under the old covenant the law was given on the day of Pentecost. So it was fitting that the legislation of the Holy Spirit should be given on the same day on which the law was given on tablets, but now written on the heart and not on tablets. That is why, setting the new things against the old legislation, he says: "You are our letter, written not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts." On the day of Pentecost the people received the law in the wilderness of Sinai. And notice how precise the count is. On the fourteenth day of the first month, reckoned by the moon, the children of Israel went out of Egypt, when they kept the unleavened bread and the mystery of the Passover. Count from the fourteenth to the end of the month, that is, seventeen days, then the thirty days of the second month. That makes the third day of the third month the fiftieth day, the feast counted from the unleavened bread of the Passover. So from the fourteenth to the third of the third month there are fifty days. That is why it says: "And in the third month after they had gone out of Egypt, the Lord said to Moses: Go down and sanctify the people today and tomorrow." He spoke to him at the new moon, for it says that on the third day the Lord will appear on Mount Sinai. Pay attention, I beg you. If the law was given on the fiftieth day, when God appeared and gave the law and Moses received the tablets, then the grace of the Spirit had to be given on the same day as the old law. In this way the authority of the Spirit would be shown and the appearing of God explained. It would also be shown that the nature of the Godhead is undivided, and that in the Old and the New and at different times it works one harmony among the divine words. When the Saviour was about to accomplish his holy passion, he would not consent to give himself up to it at any other time than the time when the lamb was sacrificed, so that he might join the truth to the very type. In the same way, the coming of the Holy Spirit would not consent to be given at any other time than the time when the law was given, so that it might be shown that the Holy Spirit gave the law both then and now. For the Holy Spirit gives law as the one who reigns over all things. The royal nature, which has the authority of the Godhead, also gives law. That he gives law, hear Moses commanding: "Remember the law of the Lord your God." Christ gives law, since his is a royal nature, an undivided Godhead. Paul says: "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." The Holy Spirit gives law, and Paul bears witness: "For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free." And see the wonder. When the law was being given, Moses' face was glorified. He came down from the mountain like the sun, with rays shining from his face. Someone might look at that ancient story, see Moses' glorified face, and think that legislation superior to the law given by the Holy Spirit. To prevent this, Paul will not allow even that they are equal. He shows the great superiority of the gospel, saying: "Not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts"; "not of the letter but of the Spirit. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." The law given in letters kills. "Let the murderer be put to death," says the law, and "let the adulterer be punished." But grace came in. It does not destroy sinners but gives them life through repentance. That is why Scripture calls the ordinance of the law "the letter that kills" and the law of the Spirit "the Spirit that gives life." Pay attention, I beg you. Then, since Moses' glorified face had been brought in for comparison, Paul says: "For if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with glory..." He does not call the law death. He means the punishment that the law lays down. "For if the ministry of death came with glory, much more does the ministry of the Spirit abound in glory." Then he presents the law as passing away, but the gospel law of the Spirit as remaining forever. Since the law was becoming inactive and coming to its end, while the grace of the gospel spread out through all the ages, Paul says: "For if what was passing away came with glory, much more does what remains abide in glory." Pay attention, then: "The letter kills," that is, it punishes sinners. "But the Spirit gives life." It opens a road of repentance and gives life to the man who has sinned. Every sin makes the sinner dead, but repentance grants him renewal and brings him into the ranks of the living. So he says, "The Spirit gives life," as Paul also says: "And when we were dead in our trespasses, he made us alive together with Christ."

So, since the power of the Spirit had to shine forth on the same day on which the law was given, hear what the writer of the Acts of the Apostles says: "And when the day of Pentecost was being fulfilled, they were all together with one accord in one place." But I beg you, pay close attention, so that you may learn how the apostles teach us to look to them and receive from them the ray of the holy light. In the Old Testament the law was given on the day of Pentecost. After they entered the land of promise, the feast had this symbol. It was not possible for a law to be given every year. The lamb was sacrificed every year, but a law was not given every year, for the things of the law did not change. So this was the symbol of the feasts: the firstfruits of the new crops and sheaves of new ears of grain were offered to God. That too was a symbol of this feast. First, the law was given then, and now there is a second law. Second, on the day of Pentecost sheaves of the new crops were gathered, and things that had been scattered came together into one sight. In the same way, on this day people from every nation under heaven, from different nations, "Parthians and Medes and Elamites," were to come together into one sheaf of godliness and be brought to God through the apostolic word. The sheaf of grain prefigured this, to foreshadow the sheaves of souls taken from different lands and brought to God as one firstfruits of the harvest. There were firstfruits then, and there are firstfruits now. You, the farmer, love everything gathered on the threshing floor, but you prize the first ear of grain that appears above the rest. You rejoice at a winepress full of grapes, yet that whole mass of grapes does not delight you as much as the single first grape that appears and gives a glimpse of the promise to come. In the same way, God loves every soul that runs towards godliness, but he loves above all the soul that gets there before the others. For example, villages and cities have sprung up on the earth. All Christians are loved by God, but the first Christian to appear is loved above all, the first ear to sprout, the first cluster. So it was with Abraham and the fathers. Since they were the beginnings of good things, when the world had not yet been saved, God says about them: "Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel, and like an early fig I saw your fathers." So too, elsewhere, Paul explains the firstfruits that answers to the type, saying: "Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia." The type contained all these things then, but now the truth has revealed them.

But let us come to the explanation of the text, word by word. "When the day of Pentecost was being fulfilled, they were all together with one accord in one place." Where were they? In a house. They did not receive the Holy Spirit in the marketplace but in a house. For it goes on: "And suddenly there came a sound like a violent rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting." What sort of house was it? It was not on the ground floor; it was an upper room. And how do we know this? Is it not written that when the disciples had seen the Saviour off at his ascension and returned to Jerusalem, "they went up," it says, "to the upper room where they were staying," Peter and the whole company of the apostles? This upper room is the one mentioned in the Gospel, in which Christ kept the Passover. For the disciples say to the Saviour: "Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?" Christ says: "Go into the city, and you will find a man carrying a jar of water. Follow him into whatever house he enters, and say to him: The Teacher says, 'My time is near; I will keep the Passover with my disciples. Where is the place you have prepared?' And he will show you a large upper room, furnished; prepare it for me there." Do you see how he keeps the rule of both Godhead and manhood? "Ask him where the place is that he is preparing, and he will show you a large upper room." If you foretell it, why do you ask? He commands them to ask and also foretells the place so that the question will show the answer agreeing with the prediction. In this way he shows both the appearance of a man and the foreknowledge of God.

"They were all together with one accord in one place; and suddenly there came a sound from heaven." See how gloriously, how royally, and with what divine authority the Holy Spirit appears at his coming. It has often been said that the divine nature does not appear as it is, but in the measure that the sight or hearing of mortal nature can bear. "Suddenly there came a sound from heaven." "From heaven" is well said. Back then, too, the first voice from God on the mountain came from heaven, and then he came down to Mount Sinai, as Moses testifies when he says: "From heaven his voice was heard, and he showed you his great fire." So now too a sound burst forth first, and then the fire appeared. Why? So that the ancient sight might also show that the same God came then and now. "There came a sound as of a rushing wind." The wind itself was not the Holy Spirit. It was fear going ahead as an escort to prepare the apostles' souls. They were not to receive the Spirit's coming in a slack state. Braced by fear and made ready for what was strange and wondrous, they would thus become worthy of his coming. Think of someone who announces that the master is arriving. He pulls the lax and idle servants together, so that each one drops his idle posture and straightens his face and bearing for the master's coming. In the same way, the violent wind came first, shook the house, and filled it with sound. Roused to fear and renewed, and with their minds purified by fear, the apostles would become worthy of the coming of the Holy Spirit. For "the fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever." "Suddenly there came a sound from heaven." The event itself was an image of things to come. "Suddenly" points to the strangeness of the teaching. "From heaven" points to the fact that what came is above this world. "A sound" points to the trumpet of the gospel, which was to resound to the ends of the world. "For their voice has gone out into all the earth." This sound began with Christ but flourished in the apostles. And where did it sound? In the Saviour, when he was working his miracles. The Gospel says: "And a sound of him went out, a sound into all Syria." And Paul says to those who had believed: "From you the word of the Lord has sounded forth." "A sound as of a violent rushing wind." Why violent? A tremor struck the corners of the house and made a spectacle. That is why the wind was violent: to call up the image of Mount Sinai. For when God appeared on the mountain, there was darkness and gloom and tempest. So just as these terrors escorted the law back then, the laws of the Holy Spirit had to be escorted by fear, so that those receiving the laws might present themselves worthy of the lawgiver.

"It filled the whole house where they were sitting, and there appeared to them tongues as of fire, distributed among them." He did not say "of fire" but "as of fire." What appeared was not fire, but it was taken for fire. And why fire? The fire was a forerunner that roused the apostles to fear. The fire was the manifestation of the Holy Spirit. And so that you will not take it as an insult that the holy and adorable nature should appear in the form of fire, he explains the new events by those that took place through Moses. Moses says: "And the appearance of the God of Israel on Mount Sinai was like a burning fire." See how that wording also agrees: "The glory of the God of Israel was like fire." He did not say "fire" but "like fire," and here too: "There appeared tongues as of fire." "And there appeared to them tongues as of fire, distributed among them." He did not say "divided" but "distributed among them." Pay attention, I beg you, to how it happened. Tongues did not appear at once. First there was a great fire, and then the fire was cut up, as it were, and distributed into tongues. Who was dividing? What was being divided? The nature of the Spirit was not divided. The Spirit was the one dividing, and what was divided was the gift of the Spirit. For the Spirit is not divided but divides. Hear Paul: "To one," he says, "is given the word of wisdom through the same Spirit, to another faith, to another gifts of healing; but all these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who divides to each one individually as he wills." He divides; he is not divided. And again the apostle says: "God also bore witness with signs and wonders and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will." Whose will? The will of the Holy Spirit, who divides to each one individually as he wills. "There appeared to them tongues as of fire, distributed among them." Why of fire? Why tongues? Because preaching was needed, and the form was meant to express what it would do. The Spirit is given in the form of tongues for no other purpose than this: so that the apostles' preaching might flourish, and so that what the fishermen lacked by nature through want of education might be given through the tongues. Then what they spoke in various languages would carry an overflowing gift and enlighten those who heard it. The fire showed that the Spirit had the power of fire to consume all the sin that was growing wild like brushwood in the world. And just as fire has the power both to give light and to burn, the word of the apostles both enlightened those who believed and consumed those who spoke against it. Paul had such a tongue of fire. With it, at one and the same time, he enlightened the proconsul and blinded Elymas the sorcerer. By the same power he enlightened the one and blinded the other.

Then: "And it sat upon each one of them." Above the heads of all the saints one could see a fire that did not burn but sanctified and shone. Why, then, did they receive the tongues not on the mouth but on the head? It was fitting that the Spirit was not given to the tongue, that is, to the natural organ of speech. Otherwise they might be thought to bring out of their own insides and their own mouths what they did not have. Waters drawn up into the sky settle on the mountain peaks and from the heights flow down into the ravines. In the same way, the grace of the Spirit settled on the crown of the head as on a mountain. From the crown it supplied the brain, then the mouth and the heart, and from the head it filled the whole man through and through. And again, why on the head? Because the apostles were being ordained as teachers of the world, and ordination takes place in no other way than on the head. The Saviour had already appointed them apostles, but not of the world. They were entrusted with Judea alone. That is why the Saviour commanded them: "Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." But the Holy Spirit, when he came, ordained them apostles of the world and teachers of all the nations. Had they not received the grace of the Spirit, they would not have been entrusted with the mission to the world. The Master himself testifies to this in these words: "And you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth." They received the beginning from the Saviour and the completion from the Spirit. This does not mean that the Spirit is higher than the Son. The Father gave the greater things to the Son and did not lessen himself. In the same way, the Son yields the greater things to the Spirit and does not lessen his own glory. God spoke the law, and he yielded the Gospels to the Son. Is the Son then greater than the Father? It is the same nature that yields. "The Father loves the Son," and the Son honours the Father. Why do you divide a nature that cannot be split, a nature at peace with itself?

When the Holy Spirit came, they were appointed apostles of the world. The preaching was just beginning, and the apostles did not yet want to go out and preach to the nations. They were attached to their own land and held fast to their ancestral customs. So God arranged for the word to be preached by foreigners in Antioch of Syria. For there were certain Syrians and Cyrenians who had gone out from the upper room, and they spoke the word and got there before the apostles. "We ought to be ashamed: the command was ours, and others are getting ahead of us. The power of God has exposed our [?]." For this reason, when the apostles and elders learned that Antioch had received the word, they sent Barnabas and Paul to the Gentiles who had believed. They came to Antioch. After preaching, they meant to return to Jerusalem again. A colt that has not yet learned to go a long road keeps turning back to the manger. In the same way, they lingered in their old customs and shrank from the journey to the Gentiles. But the Spirit saw that they would not venture it of their own choice, but were held back by hesitation and enslaved to habit. So when Paul and his companions were about to return to Jerusalem, the Spirit said, while they were fasting: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them." He did not say "to which he commanded them to be called" but "to which I have called them." And the narrator adds: "So, sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Antioch."

I have said these things because the tongues appeared on their heads, so that the form of ordination might be shown. Why is ordination performed on the head? Because the necessary rites of the Church follow from this. For see how the practice has held from then until now. Since the teaching of the Holy Spirit is invisible, the rule of the Gospel book was devised: the Gospel is laid on the head of the bishop who is about to be ordained. And when it has been laid there, what one sees is nothing other than a tongue of fire resting on the head. It is a tongue because of the preaching, and it is of fire because of the one who says: "I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish, if it is already kindled?" "It sat upon each one of them." He did not say "it was set there" or "it arrived," but "it sat." He wanted to show that every man who serves God and receives a ministry is a throne of God. He did not say "it hovered over each one" but "it sat upon them." Peter's head was a throne of the Holy Spirit, and so was Andrew's, and each of theirs alike. Pay attention, I beg you. Just as there are thrones of God and thrones of wisdom, so there are also thrones of lawlessness. That is why David says: "Shall the throne of lawlessness have fellowship with you?" "It sat," it says, "upon each one of them." One could see fire seated upon them and recognize a nature that showed one thing to the eye and brought about another by its working. "And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit." It was shown first that it sat on the head, and that from the head the whole man was filled.

“They were all filled,” it says, “with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.” Pay attention to “gave them utterance.” It is the Spirit that distributes, and the Spirit that grants speech both to the one who preaches and to the one who bears witness. No man can bear witness unless the Spirit is at work in him, and no one is a herald of God unless the Spirit supplies him. Do you want to see that no one is a herald of God who is not empowered by the Holy Spirit, and that no one can bear witness who is not strengthened by the Holy Spirit? The Savior says, as he prepares everyone for the virtue of martyrdom: “When they bring you before the courts, do not worry about how or what you will say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” And elsewhere: “For what you are to say will be given to you in that hour, as the Spirit gave.” How is it, then, that the Savior says again elsewhere: “Do not worry about what you will say, for I will give you a mouth of wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to contradict”? Because the Father gives, and the Son, and the Spirit. Here the Lord says, “I will give.” Elsewhere he says, “It is given to you by the Holy Spirit.” Where is the truth? The nature is undivided, and so is the giving. The Spirit gives; the Son gives. Does the Father, then, not give a mouth? Listen to God speaking to Moses, when Moses was making excuses about the weakness of his organs of speech and saying: “I beg you, Lord, I am slow of speech; appoint someone else who is able.” What then? “And the Lord said to Moses: Who gave man a mouth?” The Savior says: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom.” “Who made the deaf hear and the blind see? Is it not I, the Lord?” If, then, the Father says that he gives a mouth, and the Son says, “I give,” and Scripture says, “as the Spirit gave them utterance,” is it not plain even to the blind that whatever is the work of the Spirit is also the work of the Son and of the Father? Whatever belongs to the Father belongs to the whole Trinity. “As the Spirit gave them utterance.” It did not say “to speak” but “to speak out from.” For they did not speak from themselves, but from the Holy Spirit.

Furthermore, the grace of God arranged from the beginning that the word should bear fruit for the apostles. For what need was there of heralds, if there were no hearers? What need was there of seed, if the ground had not been broken up? Since, then, the firstfruits of the nations had to take their place from the very outset, the writer says: “Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem devout men, Jews, from every nation under heaven.” For the tongues were given for the sake of the gift to the nations. So the firstfruits of the nations had to receive the sign from there. “There came suddenly from heaven,” so that the crowd might be gathered by what happened. You know how curious people are: a person cannot bear not to ask, “Is it an earthquake? Is it a wind? Did God arrange this?” Then they say: “No, but the disciples of the crucified one have received the Holy Spirit.” They all began to stand there, not yet as friends, but as spectators of a strange sight. “And when this sound came, the crowd gathered and was confounded because of fear.” And to show that it was fear and the strangeness of the sight that caused the confusion, it says: “They were confounded with fear, because each one heard the apostles speaking the mighty works of God.” There is, then, a confusion that produces composure. When the fear of God confounds you, it leads you to compunction. You were confounded through the consciousness of your sins; you were set right through the hope of repentance. “And all those from the nations considered, saying to one another: Look, are not all these who are speaking Galileans?” For they were recognized because of the Savior and because of their native speech. And just as today the speech of the Cappadocians or the Bithynians cannot be hidden, but each people has some peculiarity of its own, so too the speech of the Galileans had something distinctive, and they could neither escape anyone's notice nor conceal it. Indeed, when the doorkeeper questioned Peter and he denied it, she says to him: “Truly you are one of them, for your speech gives you away.” “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in our own native language, Parthians and Medes and Elamites?” For the time being they received the gifts of fifteen tongues, as many as were needed for those present. For what need was there of the Persian tongue when no Persians were present? But just as in wars every engine and every device is prepared, yet each of them is put to work according to the need and necessity that arises, so as many tongues appeared then as there were heads of nations. Why the firstfruits of fifteen tongues? So that both the working of the Trinity might appear, and the twelve ministers as well. “And how,” it says, “do we hear them speaking the mighty works of God?” Now pay attention, please. In displaying the miracles, the apostles also joined to them the preaching of the cross. This was so that the glory that appeared might remove the suspicion of lowliness, while the grace of the cross was woven together and built up little by little, and so that what happened might testify against the suspicions of the many that what was supposed was one thing and what was at work was another. For example: the apostles spoke of this grace which they had received through the one who suffered, the crucified one, the Master of heaven, and they did not seem to be contradicting themselves. For the tongue that was present dispelled suspicion and confirmed the preaching. They spoke the mighty works of God. One could see Peter the Galilean speaking Latin, a language he had not learned, so that the ancient saying might also be fulfilled: “When he went out from Egypt, he heard a language he did not know.” The Holy Spirit arranges things so that there might be no dispute among the apostles about where each should go, and to each a tongue is given like a rule: “You speak Latin; go to Rome. You speak Persian; go to Persia.” And just as priestly ordination declares to the one being ordained the rank of his office, whether deacon or presbyter or bishop, and he cannot seize for himself any other rank than the one proclaimed over him, so the apostles too received their rule in the tongue. But since, on the other hand, they had to pass through many nations on their way to Rome, they received other tongues as auxiliaries, so to speak, while holding the first from their ordination. For each of the apostles is found speaking various tongues, since they passed through many nations, as Paul says: “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.” Peter spoke Latin, and rule over the Romans was proclaimed to him. And this was a rule and a boundary: “This is assigned to you.” Let this one go to the east; let this one go to the west and illumine the western regions; this one to the north, this one to the south.

And the heralds scattered like flashes of lightning leaping out all at once, as was said of them by the prophetic tongue: “Your lightnings lit up the world; the earth saw and was shaken.” And yet lightning does not shake the earth; an earthquake does. But since the preaching of the apostles shook the nations, who were indignant at it as at an innovation, “the earth saw and was shaken.” And how was it shaken? When Paul entered Macedonia, the earth was shaken. For the Greeks began to say: “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too.” These things became a pattern for us, so that you may never be grieved when you hear a word of insult. For nothing strange is being said: “home-wreckers,” “Christians,” “agitators.” These things were said of those luminaries: “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too.” Give a horse an open plain and let it run, and it raises neither mud nor uproar, but completes its course smoothly. Let it strike water, and it makes slippery ground and puddles; and this is inevitable, since what stands firm is not shaken. So it is with every soul that is muddy and unstable and does not receive the tread of the apostles. And the prophet cries this out: “You made your horses ride into the sea, stirring up many waters.” But to show that the royal horses bring about not only disturbance but also salvation, he says: “You mounted your horses upon the sea, and your riding is salvation.”

“And they were all amazed and perplexed, saying to one another: What does this strange thing mean? But others mocked and said: They are full of new wine.” Envy is never far from virtue. God's teaching is never without the torment that comes from the wicked. God was at work, and they put it down to drunkenness. The fruit of the Holy Spirit was taken for drunkenness. See how wickedness is refuted both by the season and by the hour. Where would new wine come from at Pentecost? For “gleukos” means new wine. But falsehood is blind; it does not know how it lies. And then: does drunkenness give different tongues, or does it not rather destroy even the one a person has? But see what God is contriving. He leaves virtue alone for a while, so that first the crowd of mockers might gather, and then the power of the saints might shine out, and so their working might be shown laying siege to the falsehood. Or do you not know that many people, aware of someone's excellence in speech or character or way of life, often shrink even from coming into his sight, lest they be struck to the heart, reproved by his very face? Had the mockery not been conceived, the Jews would have declined to come in and listen. God permitted it, so that the mockery might gather many and grace might catch them all. The Savior does this in his own case too. He went to raise the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, who had died. And since he knew the slanderousness of the Jews and the excess of their ingratitude, and that they were capable of denying the resurrection, he went in, found them mourning, and said to them: “Do not weep; the girl is not dead, but sleeping.” They laughed at him, saying: “She is dead. Why are you mocking the crowd?” “Consider,” they say, “how he lies. Everyone sees that she is dead, and he says she is not dead; he denies what is admitted.” And they laughed at him, so that their laughter might first establish an agreement. They laughed at him. And in countering their malice he did not lie. For to God nothing dies. What is about to be raised has not died. She is sleeping, for she is about to be awakened. As with “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep,” where death was taken to mean sleep, so here too: “She is not dead, but sleeping; and they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.” When he had gathered the crowd, he says to them: “She is not dead.” Why? If he had gone in and raised the girl, the Jews would have said that they had been in collusion with him and that she had not been dead. But he lets himself be mocked, so that once they had admitted that she was dead, they could no longer deny it after the resurrection. So it is here too: “They are full of new wine.” “But Peter,” it says, “standing with the eleven, raised his voice.” Learn, then, what the Holy Spirit accomplishes. See who Peter was before grace and who he became after grace. Before he received the tongues of fire, when he was questioned by one wretched slave girl he was afraid and said, “I do not know the man.” There, one slave girl and great cowardice; here, a countless crowd and his voice raised with boldness. Why? “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” “Peter, standing with the eleven, raised his voice and spoke out to them.” It did not say “spoke” but “spoke out.” In addition to what he spoke in a tongue, he added his teaching: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words.” Consider the man who was then afraid, now speaking boldly. Consider the man who was then timid, now courageous. “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day.” “Not even the hour,” he says, “made you ashamed.” Are men drunk at the third hour who have been entrusted with the word, who have taken up the common business of the whole world? The heralds of the word, those entrusted with the heavenly teaching, are cautious even about taking wine at the proper time. We, for our part, exposed the falsehood from the season of the fruits; but Peter exposed it from the hour as well.

"For these men are not drunk, as you suppose," he says, "but this is what is written in the prophet Joel." You see that nothing but prophetic testimony can resolve the difficulties. I say this so that, when a heretic stirs up trouble against an orthodox believer and one of the hard questions comes up, you do not take refuge in reasonings. For the notions of reasoning are put forward and overturned, built up and torn down. But who can break the voice of God? Reasoning can be broken; Scripture cannot be broken. Listen to the Lord: "Is it not written in your law, 'I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High'?" And he adds: "If then he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken."

While they were at a loss, Peter says: "This is what was spoken through the prophet Joel." What does "Joel" mean? "Of the Lord God." "For it shall be," he says, "in the last days, says God, that I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh." He did not say, "I will pour out my Spirit," but "of my Spirit." Is the Spirit poured out? Not at all; it is the gift of the Spirit. "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams." See how varied is the revelation of the Holy Spirit. One prophesies, having the grace of the Spirit. Another, lacking the strength to serve in such a work, receives the gift of visions, as Peter saw the sheet at the sixth hour, and as Cornelius saw the angel at the ninth hour. What is in the heart is not called a sight but a vision. One person sees a vision in one way, as it says, "Walk as one who sees"; the one who merely sees a spectacle with his eyes sees in another way. Another again is instructed by a dream through the imagination. The first is prophecy, the second vision, the third dream. The old men saw dreams, since old age is too weak for service. Yet even if it cannot serve, let it not be scorned, because of its virtue.

"And even upon my servants," he says, "I will pour out of my Spirit, and they shall prophesy; and I will give signs in the heaven above and on the earth below: blood and fire." It was said earlier too, when we took up the discourse on the cross and, as far as we were able, unfolded the holy passion in contemplation, that two strange things were given: blood and fire. Fire is the coming of the Holy Spirit; blood is the grace that came forth from his side. For it is impossible for blood to flow from a dead body, since it congeals. That is why God places it among the signs: "I will give signs in the heaven above and on the earth below: blood and fire and vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood." Many have thought that he spoke of blood with reference to the moon and not to the side. But he means the blood which the Jews shed and drew down upon themselves when they said, "His blood be on us and on our children." And after killing him they deny it. For wickedness always passes sentence against itself, then repents and takes back its own words. Those who said, "His blood be on us," say to the apostles, "Why do you want to bring this man's blood upon us?" "The sun," he says, "shall be darkened, and the moon, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes." For the first coming, the one in the flesh, the coming to teach, was lowly; but the second is glorious, when that holy body no longer appears in humility but as the radiance of flashing light. That is why he says, "the great day of the Lord."

We have often said that it is God who says, "I will pour out of my Spirit." Say to the Jew: if there is one person, and one divine name, and he is speaking about himself, why did he not say, "before my day comes"? Consider the one who says: "I will pour out of my Spirit and give signs before the day of the Lord comes, and it shall be that whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved"—calling the Savior "Lord," as Paul says: "For the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him. For whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved." And to show that he is speaking of Christ, he adds: "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they preach unless they are sent?" The coming of the Holy Spirit has been described as far as we are able: that it is royal, that it is glorious, that it is undivided, that it is peaceful. For a nature is at peace with itself, even when the Son works toward the Father. The Savior leads us up; he calls us to the Father, saying: "Whoever does the will of my Father, this one is my brother and sister and mother." So the Son points to the Father. And the Father says: "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." And just as the Father bears witness to the Son, so in turn the Son bears witness to the Spirit, saying: "But when the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will remind you of all things and will guide you into all the truth." Pay attention, then. The Holy Spirit came upon the apostles and spoke in them. The saints who saw it at the time did not know how to grasp what they were contemplating. Who is the one speaking in these men? God? The event itself showed that it was God. But the apostles did not allow it to be understood simply as God, but with the name of the Holy Spirit. For since everyone knew the name of God, but no one knew that of the Son and of the Spirit, the apostles left aside what was already acknowledged and brought forward what had been hidden. Everyone knew that God had spoken in the prophets; the apostles were eager to refer the prophecies to the Son and the Spirit. When Peter was about to appoint someone in place of Judas the betrayer, he says: "Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the mouth of David." You see how he refers the prophecies to the Spirit. Then it was the Holy Spirit who spoke; now Peter alone, the holy one, said that it was spoken through the mouth of David by the Holy Spirit. How then does Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, say: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and brought redemption to his people, and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke through the mouth of all his holy ones"? If the Baptist's father says, "God spoke through the prophets," and Peter says, "The Holy Spirit spoke," it is clear that the Spirit is God, as Peter testifies and John's father explains. Undivided is the nature, unparted the glory, unsplit the kingdom, united the power. The Father wills, the Son consents; the Son desires, the Father decrees; the Spirit sets the seal. The Father commands, the Son confirms. In the vision of the sheet the Father says to Peter, "Rise, Peter, kill and eat," and Peter says, "By no means, Lord; I have never eaten anything common or unclean." Then the voice of God says, "What God has cleansed, you must not call common." And Peter says, "God has shown me too." Then it adds: "The Holy Spirit said to Peter: Go down and go with them, without hesitating at all." The Spirit says, "I have sent them"; Peter says, "God has shown me too." Do you see that the nature is undivided?

When he speaks, is ordinary reasoning to put up a fight? If I speak, I do not say "Unbegotten" but "Father." The heretic says, "I say 'Unbegotten.'" You say to him: "Are we wiser than God? He did not say, 'Make disciples in the name of the Unbegotten and the Begotten.' Do you insult the Master's word and adopt a foreign one? The altar would not tolerate strange fire, and will the baptistery tolerate strange words?" No one contradicts God, if he is of God. I did not say, "if the words are God's," but "if the one who hears is of God." No one contradicts God; it is impossible. When God said to Peter, "Rise, Peter, kill and eat; nothing is common or unclean," Peter did not object and say: "You laid down the law: eat this and do not eat that. Do you separate them there and join them here? If the law is true, these things are not clean." If it had been a man, such an argument would have had room; but where it is God, there is no arguing back. That is why Peter says: "You know how unlawful it is for a Jewish man to associate with a foreigner; but God has shown me too that I should call no man common or unclean." What you have heard from God, do not reason over. God has spoken: obey, and do not contradict the truth. That is why Solomon too says: "Child, do not contradict the truth in any way."

You have heard God the Father, you have heard the Son, you have heard the Spirit. Why do you split what cannot be divided? God says, "I will pour out of my Spirit," and you make what he says foreign to him. "'My Spirit,'" says the heretic, "is said by appropriation and not by nature, just as 'my servant' is said." Grant that the word "my" is common to both: it expresses both nature and appropriation. I ask, then: how does he speak of the Spirit? As something appropriated? As something acknowledged as his own? For angels and heaven and earth are also called God's, not by nature but by appropriation. Do you want to see that the Spirit is God's not by a servant's belonging but by the freedom of nature? Listen to Paul: "No one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit that is in him." If the spirit in us is foreign to us, then the Spirit of God is also foreign to him and his servant. "I will pour out of my Spirit." And elsewhere: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host." And again, proclaiming the Trinity plainly, he says: "Be strong, Zerubbabel, for I am with you, and my good Word, and my Spirit is in your midst." This is the living grace, the undivided power, the unparted kingdom that was with them and is with us and guards all. To it be glory and power, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
